source: Kandal Provincial Department of Agriculture (មន្ទីរកសិកម្មខេត្តកណ្តាល), "ដំណំពោត" (Corn Crop / Zea mays production manual), 2015
text:
Gibberella ear and stalk rot (ជម្ងឺរលួយផ្លែ និងដើមពោត, Gibberella Ear and Stalk Rot): ear rot from this disease is recognized by a reddish-pink/purple mold color that starts from the tip of the ear at the silk-attachment end. Gibberella stalk rot shows a similar reddish-pink discoloration and can develop before symptoms of ear rot become visible, and it also causes overall poor plant health, leading to lodging (stalks falling over), since the rot weakens stalk strength.

This disease and stalk rot have been reported occurring in corn-growing regions of the United States. The fungus develops well in cool conditions, below about 72 degrees Fahrenheit (approximately 35 degrees Celsius). When conditions are conducive, infection of the ear can occur within about 2 weeks of silk emergence and continues to develop as the ear matures. This disease can also occur without a preceding insect wound; it is not necessarily dependent on insect damage. During the months of June and July there is generally less of a problem, but risk rises in August and September, which are months more conducive to Gibberella disease development, especially when ear infection has occurred through the silk channel.

Prevention and control measures include:
- Use disease-resistant/tolerant hybrid varieties where available.
- Choose planting dates carefully.
- Manage the crop appropriately to reduce plant stress.
- Keep the field clean and free of leftover crop debris.
- Control insect pests, since insect damage can increase disease entry points.
